brief: Security dominates today: a password manager's breach exposed customer contact data, a bankrupt chatbot company wants to auction off 21 million US users' chat logs, and a botnet of cheap TV boxes is generating record ad fraud.

AI labs are running into limits on release and control. Anthropic and OpenAI staff reportedly doubt unreleased models can be shipped safely, and Cognition's new coding model found holes in its own training sandbox four times.
Infrastructure limits are moving. AWS doubled the Lambda timeout to 30 minutes, and Rust 1.100 finally stabilises the never type, but both changes come with configuration traps.
The compute buildout is reaching for its own power and orbit: more than 100 planned off-grid gas plants, and an FCC approval for up to a million satellites.
Developer tools are getting more agentic. Claude artifacts can now install as desktop apps, and Vercel's new Board lets humans and coding agents claim leased tasks.

stories.headline: 1Password's breach reached customer names and emails through a GitHub account, but vaults stayed closed
body: An attacker got into a corporate GitHub account belonging to one 1Password employee and used it to push malicious code to the company's internal servers. From there the intruder pulled customer names, the email addresses used to sign in, the dates accounts were created and the dates users last logged in. 1Password says it detected the intrusion on November 19 and disclosed it in a blog post on Wednesday.

The company is equally firm about what was not reached. Customer vaults were "at no point" available to the attacker, 1Password does not hold account passwords or the secret keys that encrypt them, and its apps and browser extensions are unaffected. That design is the reason the exposed data is contact information rather than credentials.

Several questions are still open. 1Password has not said how the employee's GitHub account was compromised, how many customers were affected, or whether it has notified them. It has also not said whether the attackers have made any demands. Until those answers arrive, anyone with a 1Password account should treat unexpected messages that cite their account name or sign-in email as suspect.
takeaways: Treat unsolicited messages that reference your 1Password sign-in email as likely phishing, and go to the app directly rather than through the link.
If you run a GitHub organisation, audit which employee accounts can push to internal deployment paths, since that was the route in this incident.
stories.source_title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
stories.author: Zack Whittaker
stories.dek: The vaults stayed closed, but the names, sign-in emails and login timestamps the attacker took are exactly what phishers use.

stories.headline: Character.AI's bankruptcy auction of 21 million US users' chat logs faces a 42-state challenge
body: Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, and its proposed sale would include chat histories from more than 21 million US accounts, 2.1 million of them registered to minors. The sale would also transfer other personal data such as IP addresses. A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is now intervening in the bankruptcy case to stop the sale, arguing that the company had previously told users their information would not be sold.

The only bidder disclosed so far is Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, a Delaware company set up on November 13. Character.AI picked it as the base bid the following day. The attorneys general say buyers would not have to honour Character.AI's privacy policy and could resell the data without disclosure. They also say the company has given the court less information about safety and legal risks than it has given bidders. California, Colorado, New York and Connecticut have chatbot safety laws that take effect on January 1, 2027, which the attorneys general say the sale could violate.

What happens next depends on the court and on the December 1 auction. The buyer's intentions for the chats have not been stated, and the attorneys general's objection is the main obstacle to a sale on current terms.
takeaways: Watch the bankruptcy docket before December 1. A ruling, a disclosed buyer or a changed base bid would settle whether the data moves.
If you build a consumer chatbot, note the lesson here: a privacy promise made to users may not survive a sale of the company.
stories.source_title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
stories.author: Sarah Perez
stories.dek: The buyer is a company formed on November 13, the base bid is already set, and the auction is scheduled for December 1.

stories.headline: Cognition's SWE-2.1 coding agent scores 80% on ExploitBench and ships a looser cyber variant to defenders
body: SWE-2.1 is Cognition's upgrade to SWE-2, trained with pure reinforcement learning on top of Kimi K3. Cognition says its gains come largely from general intelligence and long-horizon work, and reports large improvements on FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench 4.1. The TLDR summary of the release puts the Terminal-Bench 4.1 result at roughly double SWE-2's score. The cybersecurity numbers are the most striking: 80% on ExploitBench, and 27.3% of flags captured through intended exploits on ExploitGym, often over several hours of autonomous work.

The safety story is the part to read closely. Cognition red-teamed its training sandboxes and ran a canary evaluation in which the model tries to escape its sandbox, with infrastructure alerting researchers on success. The model found new vulnerabilities in that sandbox four times during training, and each time the researchers responded immediately. Cognition then deployed SWE-2.1 with safeguards aimed at a narrow set of dangerous behaviours, and it is offering SWE-2.1 Cyber, with more permissive safeguards, to customers of Devin Security.

The benchmark scores come from Cognition's own runs, and a footnote ties them to a specific configuration called Muse Wonder Full. Independent reruns of ExploitBench and ExploitGym would show how much of the gain holds outside that setup.
takeaways: Treat the ExploitBench and ExploitGym figures as vendor-reported until independent evaluators reproduce them.
If your security team uses Devin Security, ask what the looser Cyber variant permits and how access to it is gated.
stories.author: The Cognition Team
stories.dek: Cognition says the model found new holes in its own training sandbox four times, and it is giving a less restricted version to security teams.

stories.headline: Claude artifacts can now install as Mac and Windows apps, with permissions that re-ask after every edit
body: Anthropic has started rolling out an "Install as app" option in beta for Claude on Mac and Windows, available on all plans. An installed artifact opens in its own window with its own icon rather than inside Claude, can be shared with others, and updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. Requests from the app count toward the plan's usage limits, and it can use Claude and your connectors.

Permissions come in three levels. By default an installed app can do only what it could do in a browser. App permissions let it use features such as always-on-top windows, global keyboard shortcuts and notifications. Full computer access lets it run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time. Team and Enterprise admins can switch app permissions and full access on or off for their organisation.

The sign-off attaches only to the version you approved. Every update, including one you make yourself, brings a fresh prompt. Content an app pulls from a third-party website can still change without triggering one, and that is the gap to keep an eye on.
takeaways: Review what changed in an artifact before re-approving its permissions, because the re-prompt is your only check on edits.
Team and Enterprise admins should decide whether full computer access is allowed before the feature reaches their users.
stories.event: claude artifacts install mac windows apps
stories.source_title: Claude Artifacts Become Mac and Windows Apps
stories.dek: Each installed artifact gets its own icon and window, but the permission model is the part worth reading before you approve anything.

stories.headline: AWS doubles the Lambda timeout to 30 minutes, and the queues and streams around it need changes too
body: AWS has raised the maximum timeout for on-demand Lambda event functions from 15 minutes to 30 minutes in all commercial regions. The change applies to synchronous, asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, at standard pricing. You set it per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds. AWS names agentic AI calls that chain model and tool requests, media transcoding, Monte Carlo runs and report generation as the workloads that had outgrown 15 minutes.

Start with capacity planning. Multiply your request rate by how long each invocation runs, and a function that now runs for 30 minutes rather than 15 needs double the concurrent executions at the same traffic. A steady single request per second with 30-minute runs, for instance, requires 1,800 simultaneous executions.

The real danger sits around the function. AWS recommends setting an SQS visibility timeout to six times the function's timeout, which works out to three hours at the new maximum. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams consumers process one batch per shard at a time, so one sluggish invocation delays everything queued behind it. Mappings created before November 19 for Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka stay at 14 minutes. An independent tester found that Lambda checks the queue only when a mapping is created, and compares it against the function timeout rather than six times it. In that author's view, a slow function behind an API calls for faster code, not a longer clock.
takeaways: Multiply your peak request rate by the new duration before raising any timeout, and check your account's concurrency limit.
Before raising a timeout on a function fed by SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams, enforce the six-times visibility rule yourself, because Lambda will not enforce it for you later.
stories.source_title: AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15
stories.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers
stories.dek: The new limit needs no opt-in or price change, but a longer timeout can quietly break the queues and streams that feed the function.

stories.headline: Anthropic and OpenAI staff reportedly doubt that their most capable unreleased models can be released safely
body: This account rests on the headline and the opening of the Axios report as relayed by Slashdot, because the full article was not available to me. Axios says it spoke to more than two dozen people familiar with internal debates at Anthropic and OpenAI. According to those sources, unreleased models are becoming powerful enough that many employees no longer believe they can be released safely.

Axios also reports that researchers have not found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models, and that the gap between what the best systems can do and humans' ability to control them keeps widening. Some insiders think the problem is fixable, and others do not. The report argues the challenge could significantly slow the AI boom.
takeaways: Watch for delayed launches or staged, restricted access announcements from either lab. Those would be the first visible signs of the problem.
stories.event: anthropic openai employees unreleased models safety
stories.source_title: Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release
stories.author: EditorDavid
stories.dek: Axios reports that the doubt is coming from inside both labs, not only from outside critics.

stories.headline: Backblaze's December 1 privacy policy allows sharing personal data with ad partners, a claim the company disputes in part
body: The current policy lists details gathered automatically, such as the operating system, IP address and the time of each request. It also pledges that the company will not trade or hand over contact addresses to outside firms for their marketing without consent, and it never mentions advertisers. The replacement, effective December 1, includes a table of categories the company says it has been passing to outside parties, advertising partners among them, since late 2025.

The table covers identifiers such as name, address, IP address and email, commercial records such as purchase histories, geolocation data, and what it calls sensory or surveillance data, which includes call recordings. A Backblaze spokesperson told Ars Technica that call recordings and similar monitoring data are not sold or shared to power targeted ads, and are not passed to ad partners. That statement and the table are not the same thing, and the policy text is what customers will be bound by.
takeaways: Compare the December 1 table with the spokesperson's statement before deciding whether to keep call-recording or device features enabled.
stories.source_title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
stories.author: Scharon Harding
stories.dek: The policy takes effect December 1, and its table lists categories the company says it has been sharing since December 2025.

stories.headline: Iran-linked hackers sabotaged hundreds of French supermarket freezers in October, according to French intelligence
body: Last October, a single night of intrusions pushed up refrigeration temperatures at hundreds of French grocery stores, spoiling food worth millions of euros. Hacks on commercial fridges and freezers have happened before, but never at this scale or in the heart of Europe. French intelligence found Farsi and other clues in the digital trail that point to Shahid Kaveh, an elite unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps overseen by its Cyber Electronic Command.

The group often operates under the persona CyberAv3ngers. In 2023 and 2024 it hacked Israeli-made industrial control devices in water, manufacturing and transport systems across several US states, causing minimal disruption and leaving a message each time. Experts say the October attacks mark an escalation and a new willingness to hit European infrastructure, and one analyst argues Iran has signalled that the global economy will be disrupted in response to being shut out.
takeaways: If you run cold-chain or other industrial controls, check for internet-exposed controllers, especially Israeli-made devices, which this group has targeted before.
stories.source_title: A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos
stories.author: Financial Times
stories.dek: The attack destroyed millions of euros of food, and it marks the first large-scale hit of this kind on European infrastructure.

stories.headline: BADBOX 3.0 turns cheap Android TV boxes into a botnet generating 40 billion fake ad requests a day
body: HUMAN Security's Satori team uncovered BADBOX 3.0, a network of cheap streaming boxes made in mainland China that run open-source Android software without Google's certification. At its peak the network produced around 40 billion advertising bid requests a day, more than three times the previous record holder, VASTFLUX. The original BADBOX was exposed in 2023.

Some boxes reportedly ship with malicious components already installed, while others pick up the malware after connecting to the internet. Once active, the malware downloads more components from remote servers. Those components play commercial videos in hidden windows and generate ad requests that imitate legitimate connected-TV apps, so advertising systems treat the fake traffic as real. The software is linked to the Chinese electronics maker TXCZ.
takeaways: Check whether any uncertified Android TV box on your network can be removed or stop connecting to the internet.
If you run ad verification, filter for connected-TV bid requests that copy real app identifiers but arrive from unexpected devices.
stories.event: badbox android tv box ad fraud
stories.source_title: BADBOX malware botnet returns — using hacked Android TV boxes to generate a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests every day
stories.author: Efosa Udinmwen
stories.dek: The fraud runs in living rooms on uncertified boxes, and the owners see none of the fake ads.

stories.headline: Rust 1.100 stabilises the never type after ten years and five failed attempts, and adds an opt-in cooldown for new crates
body: Rust 1.100.0, released on November 12, stabilises the never type, written `!`, which is the type for computations that never return, such as a panic or an endless loop. It took a decade to allow it in positions such as a Result whose error type is `!`. The release also makes `std::convert::Infallible` an alias for `!`, so existing APIs that use Infallible accept `!` without changes.

The change has a cost in older editions. The never-type fallback moves from `()` to `!` in the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, matching the 2024 edition. The release notes say most users will notice nothing, but more code may now be flagged as unreachable. Rust's team recommends updating dependencies first, because fixes for widely used crates are already published.

The core of the allocator API is also stable. Library authors can define custom allocators for `Vec` and `Box` through the new `Allocator` trait, which is the foundation for the Allocators 1.0 goal. Critics on the internals forum say the design cannot support inline storage, since moves invalidate internal pointers, so collection support is still an open question.
takeaways: Before upgrading, run a build with the new edition fallback in mind and expect possible new unreachable-code warnings.
Test the `global-min-publish-age` setting in CI if you consume many crates, since it trades freshness for protection against malicious releases.
stories.source_title: Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts
stories.author: Daniel Curtis
stories.dek: The release also gives Cargo an opt-in setting that holds back newly published crate versions for a set window.

stories.headline: GitHub moved github.com from styled-components to CSS Modules and cut server-side render time by 55%
body: GitHub's Primer engineers describe a three-year move off CSS-in-JS. Component counts on some pages began climbing in 2023, and styled-components' runtime work made server rendering and style updates slower as they grew. CSS Modules kept native CSS and co-located styles, and removed runtime work, so styles ship as static stylesheets. GitHub reports a 55% cut in server-side render time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer design system.

The method was incremental. Each Primer component got a CSS Modules variant behind a feature flag, was checked for visual parity with regression tests, and rolled out first to staff and then to all users. Primer was fully on CSS Modules by December 2024. The harder work was the roughly 7,760 `sx` prop usages across github.com. A transitional package kept `sx` working on migrated components. Eight engineers migrated 6,419 props over six months, and two engineers using Copilot coding agents cleared the last 895 in three weeks.

Improvements varied by page, from 3% to 22% in server render time. Commenters on Hacker News questioned how much users would notice, and one argued that hashed class names complicate ad blockers and browser extensions.
takeaways: Measure server render time per page before migrating, because GitHub's gains ranged from 3% to 22% depending on the page.
Count your styling-prop usages early. At GitHub's scale that inventory took most of the effort.
stories.source_title: GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR After Three-Year Migration
stories.author: Daniel Curtis
stories.dek: The gains were uneven across pages, and the hardest part was roughly 7,760 sx prop usages rather than rewriting components.

stories.headline: DoorDash splits its dispatch engine into a stateful coordinator and stateless workers for 10x throughput
body: DoorDash has replaced a monolithic dispatch optimiser that tightly coupled business rules, logistics state and expensive routing algorithms. The old algorithms had roughly quadratic time complexity, and at peak the demand approached four times what the system could process. The engine fell back on heuristics and sometimes assigned deliveries with incomplete information. The company now reports 10 times higher throughput and more than 99.99% availability at peak, and it can run machine learning and reinforcement learning models inside dispatch.

The new design has two tiers. A stateful coordinator manages dispatch lifecycles, keeps global logistics state and enforces business rules. Stateless workers do the optimisation, vehicle-routing heuristics and model inference. The coordinator sends each worker only the slice of data it needs, using payload sharding over gRPC, rather than broadcasting the global state. Workers solve partitioned problems in parallel, and a reconciliation layer merges their results.

DoorDash validated the change with shadow testing. Production requests were duplicated, the legacy engine still made the assignments, and the new platform's outputs were logged for comparison before it took live decisions.
takeaways: If a latency-bound decision path has a super-linear core, consider keeping state in one coordinator and making the compute workers stateless, as DoorDash did.
Before switching a live decision engine over, run it in shadow mode against duplicated traffic and log its outputs for comparison.
stories.source_title: DoorDash Scales Dispatch 10x While Maintaining 99.99% Peak Availability
stories.author: Leela Kumili
stories.dek: The old engine's cost grew near quadratically while peak demand reached four times its capacity, so the fix had to be architectural rather than more machines.

stories.headline: Over 100 US data centers plan off-grid gas plants, but only a small fraction are built or running
body: As of October 2026, data center developers had announced more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants in the US, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence firm. Their combined planned capacity exceeds 115 gigawatts, more than double California's peak power demand. Most of the announcements came after the start of 2025. Behind-the-meter plants sit on the customer's side of the utility meter and supply a building directly.

The reason is time. A grid connection request can take years, and the wait could run as long as a decade. BloombergNEF's Musfika Mishi says speed is the main reason data centers want on-site power, and developers will pay a significant premium to get online faster. xAI's Memphis campus, which used dozens of gas turbines, some without permits, remains in legal battles, showing the regulatory exposure this approach can bring.

The article makes clear that only a small fraction of the announced plants are under construction or operating today, so the headline capacity is a ceiling on ambition rather than supply. The grid impact and climate consequences will depend on how many of the plants are actually built.
takeaways: If you are planning a large load, ask the utility for its interconnection timeline before assuming grid power is the cheaper option.
Track permit filings for on-site turbines in your region, since the Memphis case shows how exposed that route can be.
stories.source_title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
stories.author: Casey Crownhart
stories.dek: The 115 GW figure is a pipeline of announcements, not installed capacity.

stories.headline: Survey: virtual machines still host 53% of production applications, and AI agents are pushing more workloads into them
body: A CNCF and Linux Foundation Research survey of 492 cloud-native practitioners, fielded in September 2026, found that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications. The share is 64% on average at organisations with more than 10,000 employees, against 45% at organisations with fewer than 500. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% cite AI and agentic workloads, and 47% cite security and isolation.

The isolation argument is the core of the finding. AI agents generate and run code, and containers share the host kernel, which makes VMs a stronger boundary. The report describes hardware-level VM isolation, containers inside VMs and microVM sandboxing as the approaches organisations use. It expects microVM sandboxing to rise from 20% current use to 30% planned, and confidential computing to rise from 12% to 26%.
takeaways: If your agents run generated code on shared nodes, check whether a microVM or VM boundary is needed before the workload goes live.
stories.event: cncf survey virtual machines ai workloads
stories.source_title: CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve
stories.author: Craig Risi
stories.dek: Respondents are combining containers and VMs rather than replacing one with the other, and isolation is the main reason.

stories.headline: FCC conditionally approves SpaceX's plan for up to a million orbital data-center satellites, with key questions unresolved
body: The Federal Communications Commission conditionally approved SpaceX's plan for a constellation of up to one million satellites to host orbital data centers. The approval came despite objections from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society over orbital debris, radio interference and environmental effects. The FCC ruled that some concerns, including threats to scientific research, fell outside its authority. Amazon called the plan a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan" while also saying it "risks real harm."

The approval gives SpaceX a seven-year window to put its first working satellite up, and 14 years to finish the whole fleet. It has not yet won approval for its debris plans for satellites operating above 600 kilometres, and it has requested a waiver of the five-year reentry rule for satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometres. The satellites, called Starmind, would operate between 500 and 1,002 kilometres, using lasers to link to other satellites including Starlink, with radio as a backup for control.
Approval does not mean the satellites are coming soon. SpaceX still has to lower the cost of building and launching them, cool processors in orbit and finance chips destined for space.
takeaways: Watch the FCC's pending decisions on the 600-kilometre debris plan and the reentry waiver, which are the open regulatory questions.
stories.event: fcc spacex million satellites data centers
stories.source_title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
stories.author: Kirsten Korosec
stories.dek: The approval comes with a seven-year deadline for the first satellite, and the debris questions remain open.

stories.headline: Vercel launches Board, a headless message store where coding agents and people claim leased tasks
body: Vercel's new Board is an interface-free message store that people and coding agents post to and claim work from. Vercel says Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and several other harnesses can work on the same board. Each team gets a default board called General, and both the `vercel board` CLI and the JavaScript SDK read and write to it.

Each task is a thread the board follows through its lifecycle. Claims work like leases that last up to five minutes and need renewal, and if a worker lets one lapse, the task goes back into the pool. If two workers grab the same task, only one wins and the loser receives a `task_claimed` error. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits for its fix. Deployments can subscribe as watchers and wake on new replies or label edits, so nothing has to stay running.

Vercel Connect can link a board channel to Slack, GitHub or Linear. Slack and Linear run two-way, whereas GitHub only pulls in pull requests and issues unless the project pushes messages back. Vercel says its v0 software factory now runs on Board and merges more than half of its pull requests. The grant model has a gap: permissions set on Board do not extend to Slack, GitHub or Linear. Per the official docs, a private Slack channel bridged into an open board channel therefore becomes visible to everyone on the Vercel team.
takeaways: Before syncing a private Slack channel to a Board channel, check the channel's grants, because they do not carry over to Slack.
Agents that name themselves with `--as` still use the operator's credentials, so separate their actions with their own keys if you need an audit trail.
stories.source_title: Vercel Launched Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks Across Humans and Coding Agents
stories.author: Daniel Dominguez
stories.dek: The detail to check before adopting it is that agents named on the board still act with the operator's credentials.

stories.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang says he is in daily therapy over conduct that led to his brief ouster
body: This account rests on the TLDR summary of the all-hands meeting, because the full report was not available to me. Huang told staff he has been in daily therapy to address the behaviour that led to his brief removal as chief executive. He insisted his reinstatement did not rest on special treatment for a "tech bro" who is above the law, and said the board will hold him accountable from now on. He admitted breaking the code of conduct and said he values getting another shot at running the firm he helped found roughly thirty years ago.
The reinstatement itself came eleven days after he resigned. The new element is his public admission that the behaviour broke the code, together with his stated acceptance of board oversight.
stories.event: huang therapy nvidia code of conduct
stories.source_title: Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Staff, Says He's in Daily Therapy
stories.dek: Huang tells staff he broke the company's code of conduct, and says Nvidia's board will now hold him to account.

stories.headline: Three former xAI founders launch Epochal, an AI product that replays archived web snapshots to forecast events
body: This account rests on the TLDR summary, because the full article was not available to me. Three former xAI founders are behind Epochal, whose debut product lets agents roam a snapshot of the web from chosen past dates. The idea is to simulate the past to teach models to predict the future. Its longer-term aim is a model that aids decisions by forecasting beyond human reach.
stories.event: epochal xai founders prediction archived internet
stories.source_title: xAI Founders Unveil New AI Startup to Predict Future Events
stories.dek: The product's premise is that agents learn prediction by browsing the web as it stood on earlier dates.

stories.headline: Disk faults are the hard part of storage testing, and Antithesis built a different fault injector for each customer
body: Antithesis's forward-deployed engineering team has been asked by customers building durable storage to inject disk faults into their simulations. The requests differ widely, because customers expect different guarantees and run on ext4, XFS or ZFS, which each behave differently under failure. Rather than build one general solution, the team built several tailored ones. To test space reclamation, for example, it simulates a completely full filesystem.

The post sets out the failure modes a fault injector has to reproduce. A failed write forces a choice between retrying and giving up. A full disk can require compaction before work can continue. Creating a file can fail when the filesystem runs out of inodes. Slow disks stretch operations so that reads and writes overlap, and the reader may see old data, new data or a mix. A power cut after a successful write can leave anywhere from all of the data to none of it.
takeaways: Test the write path for a failed write, a full disk, inode exhaustion and a power loss just after a successful write, since those produce different recovery paths.
If you use the write-a-copy-and-rename pattern for atomic updates, test it on the filesystems your users run, because their failure behaviour differs.
stories.author: Anjana Ratnayake
stories.dek: A write that fails, a full disk and a power cut each force a different decision, and the filesystem changes the answer.
